building.local_amendments_note: The Kentucky Building Code is a statewide 'mini/maxi' code: a local government may not adopt or enforce any other building code for commercial construction. Lexington's own codes page lists the state code and links its own copy of the Fourth Edition. Chapter 5 of the Lexington-Fayette Code of Ordinances could not be opened (Municode and American Legal block automated access), so the absence of any administrative add-on there is not confirmed.

fixtures.basis: Toilet counts come from the Kentucky State Plumbing Code (815 KAR 20:191), which Section 2902.1 of the Kentucky Building Code points to. The building code is statewide and may not be replaced by a local one, and plumbing in Lexington is reviewed and permitted by the State Inspector, not by the city. Lexington's codes page lists the state plumbing code with no local amendment. The state pack's worked examples stand.
fixtures.quote: 2902.1 Minimum fixture requirements. In a building accommodating males and females, it shall be presumed that the occupants will be equally divided between males and females, unless otherwise denoted. Each building shall have the minimum fixture requirements established by 815 KAR 20:191.

permit.exempt_list_quote: 105.2 Work exempt from permit. [...] Permits shall not be required for the following: Building: 1. One-story detached accessory structures used as tool and storage sheds, playhouses, and similar uses, provided the floor area is not greater than 120 square feet (11 m2). 2. Fences not over 7 feet (2134 mm) high. 3. Oil derricks. 4. Retaining walls that are not over 4 feet (1219 mm) in height measured from the bottom of the footing to the top of the wall, unless supporting a surcharge or impounding Class I, II, or IIIA liquids. 5. Water tanks supported directly on grade if the capacity is not greater than 5,000 gallons (18 925 L) and the ratio of height to diameter or width is not greater than 2:1. 6. Sidewalks and driveways not more than 30 inches (762 mm) above adjacent grade, and not over any basement or story below and are not part of an accessible route. 7. Painting, papering, tiling, carpeting, cabinets, counter tops, and similar finish work. 8. Temporary motion picture, television, and theater stage sets and scenery. 9. Tents and membrane structures having an area of 400 square feet (37 m2) or less. 10. Shade cloth structures constructed for nursery or agricultural purposes, not including service systems. 11. Swings and other playground equipment accessory to detached one- and two-family dwellings. 12. Window awnings in Group R-3 and U occupancies, supported by an exterior wall that do not project more than 54 inches (1372 mm) from the exterior wall and do not require additional support. 13. Non-fixed and movable fixtures, cases, racks, counters, and partitions not over 5 feet 9 inches (1753 mm) in height.
permit.exempt_list_note: This is the state code's list (2018 Kentucky Building Code, Fourth Edition, Section 105.2, Building items 1 to 13, read in the official PDF). Lexington publishes no exempt-work list of its own on its permit pages.
permit.city_quote: Building permits are required, but are not limited to the following: New commercial building; New commercial addition; New paving; Commercial remodeling of any kind; Commercial fences; Retaining walls two feet or more in height; Commercial towers and satellite dish installation; Tanks for storage of all liquids and gases; Commercial canopies; Change of Use
permit.city_quote_2: The remodeling of offices, warehouses, apartments, restaurants or other types of commercial facilities requires a building permit prior to starting construction. [Permit Guide For Commercial Remodeling, Fit-Ups & Change of Use, June 26, 2019]
permit.partitions_note: Neither the state list nor the city's pages name toilet partitions. Item 13 exempts non-fixed, movable partitions not over 5 feet 9 inches; toilet partitions are anchored. Item 7 exempts 'similar finish work'. The city says 'commercial remodeling of any kind' needs a permit. The question is left to the Division of Building Inspection.

restrooms_city.note: No city rule on single-user restroom signs or shared all-gender rooms was found. The city may not amend the building code. Lexington's Fairness Ordinance (Code of Ordinances Section 2-33, Ordinance 201-99) bars discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, public accommodation and housing; its only restroom clause lets an employer designate gender-specific restrooms. It sets nothing on signs or room layout, so the state pack's bullet is kept unchanged.
restrooms_city.quote: (6) Nothing in this section shall be construed to prevent an employer from: (a) enforcing an employee dress policy which may include restricting employees from dress associated with the other gender; or (b) designating appropriate gender specific restroom or shower facilities.
restrooms_city.confidence_note: The ordinance was read in the copy the Lexington-Fayette Urban County Human Rights Commission publishes (undated compilation); the current Code of Ordinances could not be opened, so a later amendment can't be ruled out.

page.meta: Commercial bathroom partitions delivered to Lexington job sites. Price your restroom, pick a material and see the Kentucky rules Lexington enforces.
page.lead: Commercial bathroom partitions for Lexington university buildings, hospitals, schools and horse farms, shipped by freight to your job site.
page.stall_bullet: - **How many stalls:** Kentucky's plumbing rules set the number of toilets and urinals by how many people use the building. They apply statewide, and in Lexington a state plumbing inspector reviews the plans, not the city. The table below shows what that means.
page.permit_bullet: - **Permits:** Lexington's Division of Building Inspection issues building permits, and the city says commercial remodeling of any kind needs one. Kentucky's building rules exempt painting, tiling, carpeting, cabinets, counter tops and similar finish work, and movable partitions no taller than 5 feet 9 inches. Neither the state's list nor the city names toilet partitions, so ask the Division of Building Inspection (859-258-3770) whether your replacement needs one. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.install_rule: Lexington requires contractors to register with its Division of Building Inspection, and an unregistered contractor cannot get a building permit. Registration takes a city occupational business license and proof of liability and workers' compensation insurance. Kentucky does not license general contractors at state level for work like partition installation. Confirm what your project needs with the Division of Building Inspection. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.faq_install_extra: In Lexington the contractor must be registered with the city's Division of Building Inspection.
page.public_jobs_bullet: - **Public jobs:** Kentucky repealed its wage law for public construction in 2017, so a set wage applies only on federally funded jobs, under the federal Davis-Bacon Act. For a carpenter on building work in Fayette County that is $20.34 an hour plus $8.58 in benefits. Drywall, ceiling, metal stud and formwork carpenters have their own rate: $32.25 plus $18.09.
page.sales_tax_bullet: - **Sales tax:** 6% in Lexington. That is Kentucky's state rate, and there is no city or county sales tax on top.
page.buyers_extra: - **Horse farms, sales pavilions and racetracks:** solid plastic or phenolic for restrooms that are open to the weather or hosed down, with heavy-duty hardware for sale-day and race-day crowds.

page.official_names: - The rules by their official names: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design; ICC A117.1-2009 as referenced by the 2018 Kentucky Building Code, Fourth Edition, February 2024 (2015 International Building Code with Kentucky amendments, 815 KAR 7:120, in force since December 3, 2024), enforced in Fayette County by the Lexington-Fayette Urban County Government Division of Building Inspection without local amendments; Kentucky State Plumbing Code (815 KAR Chapter 20; fixture counts in 815 KAR 20:191), applied by the state's plumbing inspectors; NFPA 286 for HDPE.
notes: To confirm by phone before launch: whether a like-for-like replacement of anchored toilet partitions in an existing commercial restroom needs a Lexington building permit (Division of Building Inspection, 859-258-3770).
Lexington publishes no list of exempt work of its own; the permit bullet pairs the city's 'commercial remodeling of any kind' line with the exempt list in the statewide building code.

The Lexington-Fayette Code of Ordinances (Municode, American Legal) blocks automated access: Chapter 5 (buildings, permits, contractor registration) and the current Section 2-33 were not read there. Check in a browser that Chapter 5 adds no permit exemption and that the Fairness Ordinance has no later restroom amendment.

The city's site gives two numbers for state plumbing review: (859) 899-3244 on the commercial construction page and (859) 899-5244 on the plumbing permits page, which names the Lexington Health Department's Plumbing Program. Neither is printed on the buy page; confirm before using one.

The contractor registration text now rests on the city's Building Inspection page (read 2026-11-24), which resolves the earlier doubt that the registration page was aimed at city vendors; the ordinance itself is still unread.

The federal wage determination lists two carpenter rates. Partition installation is not named in either; the general carpenter rate ($20.34 plus $8.58, a 2015 survey rate) is given first because the higher rate covers only drywall, ceilings, metal studs and formwork.
The lead's four building types and the horse-industry buyers bullet are editorial, not sourced.

Larger buildings (offices, stores and factories for more than 100 people, all schools and care buildings, anything over three stories or 20,000 square feet) have their plans reviewed by the state as well; Lexington's guide says they still need a local permit.
